newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian leader loses press defamation case.
newsitem.headline: Croatian leader loses press defamation case.

text.p: A Croatian court on Thursday acquitted two independent journalists of defaming nationalist President Franjo Tudjman, in an unexpected boost for freedom of the press in the former Yugoslav republic.

The Zagreb Municipal Court found Viktor Ivancic and Marinko Culic, editor and lead writer respectively of the satirical and muck-raking weekly Feral Tribune, not guilty in a case lodged by state prosecutors at the behest of Tudjman.

Ivancic and Culic were the first journalists indicted under a new clause in Croatia's criminal code enacted to protect the reputation of top state officials at a time of declining government popularity.
Diplomats and opposition analysts said the measure was intended to muzzle the few independent news organisations that had managed to avoid takeovers by interests fronting for Tudjman's HDZ party.
Tudjman took offence at Feral's way of criticising his proposal that the remains of members of Croatia's World War Two Nazi puppet regime should be reburied at a monument for Serb and Jewish victims.

He also objected that Feral articles and photo montages on the subject likened him to the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, Croatian World War Two fascist strongman Ante Pavelic and Yugoslav Communist leader Josip Broz Tito.
Judge Marin Mrcela said there was no legal basis to sustain the guilt of the accused, as neither the articles nor photo montages could be interpreted as slanderous.
He said the montage was obviously absurd, and was included in the satirical supplement of the issue, while the articles merely passed judgment on aspects of political activity.
State prosecutor Visnja Loncar had argued that the trial was not about freedom of the press but "responsibility for (offensive) acts against the president of the republic".
The defendants could have been jailed for up to three years if convicted.

"This verdict supports free thought and condemns hypocrisy," defence lawyer Branko Seric told reporters. "It would be hypocritical to allow people to crack jokes at the expense of politicians in the street, but ban such humour from the press."

"The judge had the courage to deliver this verdict and we must also take into account international pressure," said Zvonimir Cicak, Croatia's top human rights activist who has been frequently denounced by the state-run media.
"We can now be 99 percent sure that Croatia will be admitted to the Council of Europe next month."

In May, the Council of Europe put Croatia's membership bid on hold partly because of a renewed right-wing campaign to silence critical media via the new defamation law, punitive taxes and other forms of legal pressure.

The Council promotes democracy and human rights in Europe, especially in the formerly communist east, and serves as the antechamber to links with the European Union which Croatia has been assiduously pursuing for years.
Feral Tribune, famed within former Yugoslavia for its irreverence, has long aggravated the government that led Croatia to independence in 1991.

Ivancic was temporarily detained in 1993 for allegedly dodging military service. A year later the government imposed a huge "pornography tax" on the weekly that could could have bankrupted it, but Ivancic had it rescinded by court action.
